drills.title: vs riclebon (784) — Modern Defense with
drills.coachNote: Black's knight on d7 was staring right at your knight on e5, aiming to trade it off and then pick up the e5 pawn with ...Qc7 next. Pushing b4 on the queenside didn't touch that at all — after Nxe5 dxe5 Qc7, your e5 pawn falls and your center caves in, costing you most of a two-pawn advantage. Nf3 simply steps the knight to safety first, keeping everything intact, and after a4 Nc4 Bxc4 dxc4 you're still comfortably better with a healthy structure. Deal with your most advanced piece before expanding elsewhere.
drills.threat: Black's knight on d7 attacks your knight on e5, and the pawn behind it is next to fall.

drills.title: vs riclebon (784) — Modern Defense with
drills.coachNote: Black wants to swap dark-squared bishops with ...Bxe5, and once you recapture dxe5 the queen jumps to c7, hitting both the fresh e5 pawn and the weak c3 pawn. Qe1 didn't prepare for any of that, so after Bxe5 dxe5 Qc7 f4 you're forced to spend a move shoring up pawns instead of pressing your edge, and a big chunk of your advantage evaporates. Bf4 sidesteps the exchange entirely by relocating the bishop before it can be traded into a weakness, and even if Black grabs the c3 pawn with Rxc3, Qd2 hits the rook at once and Rfc1 gets you full compensation. Reposition pieces before they get traded into liabilities.
drills.threat: Black's dark bishop on g7 can trade off your e5 bishop, then bring the queen to c7 to hit e5 and c3.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: White's whole plan is Rb8+, pushing your knight to a passive square, then rolling the connected c5-d6-e6 pawns while your rook on a5 sits on the wrong side of the board. Kd8 walked straight into that: after Rb8+ Nc8 c6 Rh7, those pawns crash through and your king gets exposed, turning a position where you were winning by nearly three pawns into one where White wins by five. Kc8 instead directly covers both b8 and d8, so the rook can never get behind you, leaving your rook and bishop free to handle the pawns on your terms. In pawn races like this, guard the entry squares before chasing your own plans.
drills.threat: White's rook on b6 wants Rb8+, and with your king off the back rank the c5-d6-e6 pawns start rolling.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: The point behind Rb6 is to swing onto c5, grab your pawn there, and follow with e6+ to rip open your king with tempo — that only works because the pawn on d5 is just sitting there hanging. Kd7 ignored it completely: after Rxc5 Rc8 e6+ Kd8, White wins the pawn plus a check, a three-pawn swing that starts your slide toward losing. Nxd5 grabs that hanging pawn first, and even after Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6 you trade down into a level ending instead of a bad one. When a pawn is undefended, take it before making a quiet king move.
drills.threat: White's pawn on d5 is undefended, but leave it alone and Rb6 crashes into c5 with check next.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your queen on c6 had a clean diagonal to g2, and with your rook on f2 already guarding that square, Qg2 was mate on the spot — the king had no flight squares left. Rxb2 grabbed a pawn instead, which is still crushing, but it let White play Nd2, blocking and buying time with Qc2 and Rh2, turning an instant finish into a longer squeeze before you eventually won anyway. Always scan for a forced mate before settling for a free pawn, especially when the enemy king is this boxed in.
drills.threat: White's king on g1 is boxed in by its own pawns, with almost nowhere to go if you strike the right square.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Every one of White's pieces is passive right now, and his one hope is getting a rook to e1 to contest your bishop on e5 and start freeing his position — any quiet move from you hands him that tempo for free. a6 was exactly that: a purely prophylactic pawn push, and after Re1 Rde8 b3 h5 White consolidates and your huge edge shrinks from nearly five pawns to about three. Qf3 instead drives your queen right into his camp near Kh2, forcing the passive Rd1, and after Rde8 Re1 Bd6 a4 you keep improving while he stays tied down. When you're winning big against a tangled position, look to increase the pressure rather than mark time.
drills.threat: White wants to swing a rook to e1, challenge your bishop on e5, and start untangling his tied-down pieces.

drills.coachNote: Black's plan is a discovered check: the rook drops back through c2 to c3, unmasking the bishop on f5 along the f5-b1 diagonal and dragging your king into the open no matter where it runs. Qxc4 grabs a knight but ignores that entirely — after Rc2+ Kb1 Rxc3+ Ka1, your king is boxed into the corner of an already-lost position, and the eval slides another four pawns the wrong way. Qb3 instead trades down the danger: after Rxb2 Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 you give back some material, but the mating net is gone and the king can finally breathe. When enemy pieces line up on an open diagonal to your king, fix that before grabbing material.
drills.threat: Black's rook on e2 and bishop on f5 share a diagonal toward b1 — capturing on c4 does nothing about that.

drills.coachNote: You're so far ahead that this should be routine — Black's only resource is shuffling the king between e7 and f7, hoping for imprecision. Kf4 looks just as central as Kf3, but your own follow-up shows the king having to backtrack to e3 after e4, Kf7, Ke7 anyway — that lost tempo is what let Black hold on far longer, cutting your margin roughly in half. Kf3 supports the same e3-e4 break without ever needing to retreat, so the king marches forward in one direction instead of two. Even in a completely won ending, the exact square still matters more than 'toward the center.'
drills.threat: Black has nothing but king shuffles between e7 and f7 — any loose move from your king and this trivial win gets much harder.

drills.coachNote: Your plan is simple: march the king to b5 and escort the c6-pawn home, with the bishop just sitting on the long diagonal out of the way. Bb3 crowds that same diagonal, so a move later you have to replay Ba2 anyway — and that spare tempo is exactly what let Black's king slip to f7 instead of being pushed to e8, making the win noticeably harder. Ba2 clears the king's path immediately, so Ke7, Kc4, Ke8, Kb5 flows through without a detour. Put pieces where they won't need to move twice.
drills.threat: Your king wants to march to b5 to escort the c6-pawn home, and where you place the bishop decides how fast that march goes.

drills.coachNote: Black's queen on g5 and rook on f2 are working together against your king on e1 — the knight on d2 is its only shield, and d2 is exactly the square the queen sits diagonally lined up on. Rf1 ignores all of that: it doesn't defend d2 or give your king anywhere to run, so Qxd2# lands immediately — a +5.6 position turns into instant mate in one move. Qd7+ was the fix: it forces Kf6 first, buying the tempo to then play O-O-O, tucking your king to c1 with the rook covering d1 too. When your king's stuck in the center behind one lone defender, fix that before anything else.
drills.threat: Your king's still stuck on e1, and Black's queen on g5 plus rook on f2 are eyeing d2 as the way in.

drills.title: vs osmanahma (728) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black never castled — the king's still on e8 — and the rook on h5 is out there with nothing guarding it. Qd4 centralizes but touches neither problem, so Black gets a free tempo to play Qd7, and by the time Bf4/Qh7/Qa4+ happen your huge edge has shrunk from +6.2 to barely +1. Qg6+ hits both issues at once: it's check along the g6-f7-e8 diagonal, and the queen simultaneously eyes the rook on h5. After Kd7, Qxh5 wins a whole rook outright, and Nd4+ keeps the king running. When the enemy king's stuck in the center and something's hanging, find the move that hits both together.
drills.threat: Black's king is still stuck on e8 and the rook on h5 is hanging out there completely undefended.

drills.coachNote: White's a6 and b6 pawns are two steps from the eighth rank, and the king on e4 wants to come support them the moment your rook looks away. Rc4+ feels active, but the check does nothing lasting — it just sends the king to d5, exactly where it wants to be, and after Kd5, Rc3, b7 the pawn is one step from queening with the king right behind it, cutting your winning margin nearly in half. Rc1 does the real work: it gets the rook onto the pawns' path first, so after b7, Re1+, Kd5, Rb1 you're blockading rather than chasing. Against connected passers, get your rook in front of where they're going, not behind the enemy king.

drills.coachNote: White's a6-pawn is the more advanced of the two connected passers, and right now nothing's actually attacking it — the rook on e6 is just escorting, not defending. Rc7 moves to an empty file and touches neither pawn, so White gets a free tempo to push b6, and after Rc1, b7, Ra1 you're scrambling behind a pawn already one step from queening, which is why your edge dropped by over 3 pawns. Ra7 was the move: it lands on the a6-pawn's own file, blockading and attacking it at once, tying White's pieces to its defense. Attack the more advanced of two connected passers on its own file, not an empty one.

drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, but Black's bishop on f5 is the only piece with any life left, and it's one tempo from jumping to g4 to stir up trouble. Kc6 looks like progress, but it hands Black exactly that tempo — Bg4 gets in, and after Kd6, Kf8, Re7 you're still winning, just fighting far more resistance than needed, which is how +67.7 drops to around +10. Kb4 keeps it simple: it stays close enough to restrict Black's pieces while continuing the march, and Bh3, Kc5, Kd8, Kd6, Kc8 shows the king walking straight through instead. Even in a totally won position, don't hand the opponent's only active piece a free tempo.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on f5 is one move from jumping to g4 and stirring up counterplay before you finish the job.

drills.title: vs Himanshu_Nagar04 (882) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black's whole plan is to chase your rook around — once your king leaves a4, ...Bh3 and ...Kc5 team up so the rook never gets to sit still, and by the time you're pushed into Rb2 you've handed back most of a crushing edge (this was +58 before Kb5). Rb2 right away does the same retreat, but on your own terms, so ...Bh3 Ka3 Bg4 still only gets Rh2 Kc6 — a calm regroup instead of a forced scramble. In a lopsided endgame like this, move the piece about to be harassed before the enemy king arrives and makes that decision for you.

Qh7 throws your queen into that same square first, forcing Qxh7+ Kxh7, and even with Bf4 keeping pressure, ...Re8 Rxe8 gets you a real fight instead of a mated king.
